articles.title: Duffy national address falls apart just as it started: 'This is our kind of, um, day'
articles.description: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s press conference on Saturday started disastrously. The Donald Trump appointee had only just started thanking air traffic controllers for their work during the crisis when feedback began blaring through the microphone at Transportation Department headquarters, the Washington Post reported. Duffy paused, tried again, and was forced to stop a second time. “Oh, this is not operational?” he asked. “This is our kind of, um, day.” Most news outlets cut away while staff scrambled to fix the sound, according to Mediaite. Minutes later the livestream returned, with Duffy counting from one to seven into the microphone before he pressed on, the report notes. The glitch came as airlines scrapped thousands more flights Saturday, a day after the FAA froze all departures for more than four hours. It was only the second nationwide ground stop since 9/11. Once the briefing got going, Duffy blamed contractor L3Harris. He said a router installed during a copper-to-fiber upgrade at a remote FAA site had flooded the network. He added that officials still didn’t know whether installation error or faulty equipment was at fault. L3Harris did not immediately respond to NPR’s request for comment. The appearance was Duffy’s second try at explaining the meltdown. A Friday night White House briefing alongside Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin had drawn widespread criticism, including griping from White House insiders.

Mary Peltola nears an Alaska Senate win as Democrats eye a 56th seat
articles.description: Democrat Mary Peltola has widened her lead over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska's still-undecided U.S. Senate race, moving within striking distance of an outright victory that would give Democrats their 56th Senate seat following sweeping midterm gains. As of Saturday morning, Peltola had 49.8% of the vote, compared with Sullivan's 46.1%, a margin of more than 10,000 votes. The Associated Press reported 96% of votes counted, with Peltola receiving 138,240 votes to Sullivan's 127,828. The former congresswoman gained nearly 2,000 votes on Sullivan in the latest batch of ballots, strengthening her prospects of clearing the 50% threshold needed to avoid Alaska's ranked-choice voting tabulation. Peltola's campaign declared victory Friday, insisting the Republican incumbent could no longer overcome her advantage. "There is no mathematical path for Sullivan to win this race," the campaign said in a statement posted on X. "When the remaining votes are counted, Mary will decisively be elected as Alaska’s next United States Senator," the statement read. Campaign manager Cheryl Bruce echoed that confidence in a statement to Newsweek. "As more ballots get counted, it’s clear that Mary’s victory is all but guaranteed, and Alaskans have resoundingly rejected Dan Sullivan’s D.C. self dealing," Bruce said. "Mary won today’s ballot drop by a decisive margin, and remaining votes from Anchorage, Juneau, and rural Alaska will continue to break for Mary, continuing her momentum to the United States Senate. "Alaskans are ready for a senator who fights to lower costs and takes on D.C. corruption, and when every vote is counted, Mary will deliver for Alaska," Bruce said. Sullivan's campaign, however, declined to concede. "We’re still waiting for every ballot to be counted. And we’ll see what happens from there," campaign spokesman Nate Adams told The New York Times on Friday. The race remained uncalled Saturday, with outstanding ballots potentially determining whether Peltola secures an outright majority or must prevail through ranked-choice voting. Under Alaska's system, if no candidate receives more than 50% of first-choice votes, the lowest-performing candidates are eliminated and their supporters' subsequent preferences redistributed until a winner emerges. Two minor candidates, Republican Gerald Heikes and unaffiliated Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., have collectively captured roughly 4% of the vote. Democrats recruited both candidates in an effort to weaken the incumbent's support, according to The New York Times. The Trump administration previously challenged the election over the presence of another candidate named Sullivan, arguing potential voter confusion, but the lawsuit was dismissed. Alaska has until Nov. 18 to complete its vote count, with ranked-choice tabulation to follow if necessary. A Peltola victory would represent another significant Democratic pickup in a midterm election that has already delivered the party 55 Senate seats, its largest majority since the early Obama administration. Peltola, who campaigned on "fish, family, and freedom," would become the first Alaska Native elected to the Senate and the first Democrat to win an Alaska Senate seat in nearly two decades. Her potential victory would also underscore Republican difficulties in a state President Donald Trump carried by approximately 14 percentage points in 2024, amid voter concerns over high prices, the administration's war in Iran, and tariffs affecting Alaska's economy. In another major Democratic victory in Alaska, former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, has won the state's gubernatorial election, defeating three Republican opponents in a four-way contest, according to Decision Desk HQ. Kreiss-Tomkins will succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy, becoming Alaska's youngest governor and the first Democrat elected to the office in more than two decades. His victory came after national political organizations poured millions into the contest, with Democrats benefiting from a divided Republican field despite Trump's endorsement of Bernadette Wilson. Meanwhile, Alaska's U.S. House race remains uncalled, with Republican Rep. Nick Begich III leading in a contest expected to proceed to ranked-choice tabulation. © 2026 Newsmax. All rights reserved. articles.title: Startup eyed over flight chaos funnels cash to Transportation chief's son-in-law
articles.description: The developer of a new AI system now under scrutiny as airplanes stand grounded nationwide funneled cash into the political campaign of Transportation chief Sean Duffy's son-in-law, records show. Air Space Intelligence, the contractor Duffy announced in June would develop the Federal Aviation Administration's new AI-powered air traffic management system, contributed $12,500 to the congressional campaign of U.S. Rep.-elect Michael Alfonso (R-WI) in March this year, federal records show. The contract it won was worth up to $875.9 million. The Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system launched this week, according to CNN National Security analyst Juliette Kayyem. "The FAA onboarded a new AI system 3 days ago," Kayyem wrote on X. "Hard to believe it's a coincidence." Air Space Intelligence's X account tweeted a denial that it was involved in Friday's chaotic downing of the national aviation system. "The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC," it wrote. One month after Duffy announced Air Space Intelligence's SMART would be used to cut delays and optimize airspace, Politico reported the Federal Aviation Administration was working to buy an ownership stake. It wasn't long before Congress members were raising the alarm about Air Space Intelligence and the system it was starting to unroll. "Concerningly, the nation’s frontline aviation safety workforce apparently had little to no input into SMART’s development and have received limited training and information during the current deployment process," 23 House representatives wrote last month. "The use of artificial intelligence within SMART has rightfully raised serious questions about its reliability and safety benefits."
